answer_text:
For any real number \(x\), its equivalence class is

\[
[x]=\{y\in\mathbb{R}: |x-y|\in\mathbb{Q}\}.
\]

If \(|x-y|\in\mathbb{Q}\), then \(y-x\) is either \(q\) or \(-q\) for some \(q\in\mathbb{Q}\), so \(y-x\in\mathbb{Q}\). Conversely, if \(y-x\in\mathbb{Q}\), then \(|x-y|\in\mathbb{Q}\). Therefore,

\[
[x]=x+\mathbb{Q}=\{x+q:q\in\mathbb{Q}\}.
\]

The map

\[
\mathbb{Q}\to [x],\qquad q\mapsto x+q
\]

is a bijection. Since \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countably infinite, every equivalence class has cardinality \(\aleph_0\).

Thus the only possible cardinality of an equivalence class is

\[
\boxed{\aleph_0}
\]
